pages.text: The history of technology is the story of human invention. People create new tools using new knowledge. Technology includes simple stone tools and complex engineering. Technical history is connected to science and economics. Technological change affects our culture and traditions every day.
pages.caption: The wheel, invented sometime before the 4th millennium BC, is one of the most ubiquitous and important technologies. This detail of the "Standard of Ur", c. 2500 BCE., displays a Sumerian chariot.

pages.text: During the Stone Age, humans lived with limited tools and few permanent settlements. The first tools were for survival, hunting, and food preparation. Major developments included stone weapons, fire, and clothing. Later, people found native copper before they knew how to smelt metal ores.
pages.caption: A variety of stone tools

pages.text: Ancient civilizations built great structures. The Egyptians used simple machines like ramps and levers to build massive pyramids. The Indus Valley Civilization used early city planning and plumbing. China created many early developments, including paper, the compass, and gunpowder for various uses.
pages.caption: Pont du Gard in France, a Roman aqueduct

evidence.articleCaption: Pont du Gard in France, a Roman aqueduct

pages.text: During the medieval period, water and wind power became very important for milling grain and other tasks. Medieval Europeans also invented mechanical clocks, spectacles, and vertical windmills. In navigation, new tools and sails helped lay the foundation for later exploration and global trade routes.
pages.caption: Walls at Sacsayhuaman

pages.text: The Industrial Revolution was driven by cheap energy from coal in Britain. It brought major developments in textile machinery, mining, metallurgy, and transport. Later, the Second Industrial Revolution brought rapid innovation in chemical, electrical, petroleum, and steel technologies across Europe until World War I.

The history of technology traces how humans have invented tools and techniques from simple stone implements to complex genetic engineering. Because much of technology represents applied science and resource utilization, technical history connects closely with both scientific and economic development. These changes significantly influence cultural traditions and serve as major forces for economic growth and political power.

pages.text: Ancient societies achieved remarkable engineering feats. The Egyptians utilized simple machines like ramps, wedges, and levers to construct massive pyramids using heavy limestone blocks. Meanwhile, the Indus Valley Civilization demonstrated advanced materials engineering through early city planning and plumbing, while China contributed numerous innovations including paper, the compass, and gunpowder.

pages.text: During the medieval period, water and wind power surpassed human and animal muscle power for milling grain and driving industrial processes. Later medieval European innovations included mechanical clocks, spectacles, and vertical windmills. Furthermore, new navigational instruments and rudder designs laid essential foundations for the subsequent Age of Discovery.
pages.caption: Walls at Sacsayhuaman

pages.text: The Industrial Revolution emerged in Britain, driven by abundant coal resources and characterized by rapid advancements in textiles, mining, metallurgy, and machine tools. Following a mid-century slowdown, the Second Industrial Revolution spanned from the 1860s to World War I, sparking rapid industrialization and structured research in chemical, electrical, petroleum, and steel technologies.

Technology encompasses the human invention of methods and artifacts ranging from rudimentary stone implements to contemporary information technology and genetic engineering. As an applied science dependent on resource allocation, technical history remains inextricably linked to economic and scientific evolution. Furthermore, technological shifts continually interact with societal cultural traditions while functioning as primary catalysts for economic growth and the projection of geopolitical power.

pages.text: Throughout the Paleolithic era, human populations subsisted with limited toolkits and sparse permanent settlements, centering technological efforts on survival, hunting, and sustenance preparation. Significant early breakthroughs encompassed stone implements, fire, and clothing. Metallurgical development subsequently advanced from utilizing native copper from weathered deposits to employing pottery kiln technologies that achieved sufficient temperatures for smelting arsenical bronze.

pages.text: Ancient monumental architecture reflected sophisticated empirical engineering. The Egyptians deployed fundamental simple machines—specifically the inclined plane, wedge, and lever—to position massive limestone blocks during pyramid construction. Concurrently, the Indus Valley Civilization exhibited advanced hydrology and sanitation infrastructure, whereas historical Chinese innovations yielded extensive breakthroughs, ranging from early seismological detectors and cast iron to gunpowder and deep-well drilling.
pages.caption: Pont du Gard in France, a Roman aqueduct

pages.text: Medieval economic structures experienced a pivotal transition as water and wind power eclipsed human and animal muscle as primary mechanical forces, primarily for grain milling alongside industrial applications like pulping and felting. Concurrently, medieval European ingenuity produced mechanical clocks, spectacles, and vertical windmills, while maritime advancements such as the pintle-and-gudgeon rudder and dry compass provided the foundational framework for the Age of Discovery.
pages.caption: Walls at Sacsayhuaman

pages.text: The British Industrial Revolution accelerated through abundant coal resources, generating transformative developments in metallurgy, textile machinery, and transport infrastructure. Subsequently, the Second Industrial Revolution from the 1860s until World War I inaugurated an era of intensive industrialization and structured technological research, propelling rapid advancements across chemical, electrical, petroleum, and steel sectors.
